228.s: Mrs. Powell trusts Jackie to take Bud to the Royal Roost and to Monk; Bud was damaged by electroshock.

228.t: Meeting Bud Powell through his brother Richard
228.s: Richard Powell visits the record shop and brings McLean to meet Bud, home on furlough from a mental institution.

228.s: Bud has McLean play Buzzy, McLean gets Richard Powell started and sends him to the older pianist Bob Bunyan.
228.q: Yeah, a saxophone. Yeah, I’m scared. He said, “Take it out. Can you play it?” I was like, “I know Buzzy,” because I knew that one song. So he said, “Buzzy? 9.t: Bud Powell joins and refuses to play 'that sad stuff'
9.s: Seventeen-year-old Bud Powell told Cootie he wouldn't play the theme as written; Holmes judges him a genius whose life was shortened.
9.ch: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
9.q: Oh, no. We hadn't been there... We weren't there all that time. No, we only played there a few weeks, I don't know how many weeks, and then we came out of there and we came back to the Savoy. See, we had come back to New York to the Savoy -- in New York here. And I think that's when Ken Kersey left…

9.t: Bud Powell borrowing five dollars and repaying seven
9.s: Bud borrowed money from Holmes between theatre shows and insisted on repaying with interest within twenty minutes.
9.ch: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
9.q: But he was a fine kid. He used to call me "Dad", like I'm his Daddy or something. Bud would want to borrow some money or something, because he was always broke. He'd get paid just now, and in fifteen minutes he wants to borrow something on next week's pay. I don't know what he'd do with his money.…

9.t: A White bandleader calls Bud a genius, and Cootie's string of pianists
9.s: A White orchestra leader on a train was amazed at Powell; Cootie kept changing piano players, all outstanding, and the band grew hard to handle.
9.ch: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
9.q: Anywhere. Everywhere. And we were traveling on the road, we run across... One time we run across some show people on the train (we was travelin' by train), and they was on a train from one of them small towns, and they were going to the same town we were going. So naturally, we all got acquainted.…

136.t: Sitting in with Bud Powell at Storyville

136.s: Powell came to hear her in Philadelphia and New York; Paris, Paudras and his remark that she was the best female pianist.

428.t: Bud Powell: Cootie Williams, Cafe Society and decline
428.s: Hall's memories of Powell at the Savoy Ballroom with Cootie Williams, then his decline in Philadelphia.
428.q: Oh, Bud was terrific. I worked with Bud well, Bud, he merged with Cootie Williams orchestra, the big band at the Savoy Ballroom when I was still working there.

428.t: Bud Powell beaten at Watts in Philadelphia
428.s: Hall describes the violence Powell suffered and the Philadelphia club that hired tenor players.
428.q: In Philly. They opened with Prez and then Jacquet and then Eddie Law Lockville. I don't know what happened after that. This was in '47, '46.

521.t: Birdland photo and awards to Bud Powell, Jimmy Smith and Lionel Hampton
521.s: A 1956 photo at Birdland with Teddy Reig; as Blue Note PR she presented awards to Powell, Smith and Hampton at night venues.

368.t: Quartet with George Shearing at the Clique, and Bud Powell's resentment
368.s: At the Clique club in 1948 the Pettiford All-Stars played, and Powell resented Shearing, even putting thumbtacks on his seat.
368.q: Oh yeah. Yeah, George Shearing and I, and John Levy, Denzil Best; we had a quartet at a club called the Clique. This was the late ‘40’s, I guess.

515.t: Bud Powell as composer and the damage of psychiatry

143.s: He played with Bud Powell around Harlem, loved his tunes but found him unreliable with money.
143.q: It was nice. With Bud, you know... When I came to New York, Bud was going nuts, going bananas. He was hard to deal with.

135.t: Bud Powell living in Benny Harris's house

225.t: Bud Powell and John Lewis compared
225.s: Powell was dapper and freewheeling; John Lewis and the MJQ were studied and disciplined.
225.q: Bud Powell was a very interesting jazz musician all the way down the line. Even in his years of failing health, he was still Bud Powell. Bud Powell was always Bud Powell. We can make no bones about that. He was dapper, always dapper. He always wore a shirt and tie. We were all casual. Bud Powell:…
